Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning

Haoran Xu Pragya Srivastava Xinjie Liu Siddhant Agarwal Amy Zhang The University of Texas at Austin haoran.xu@utexas.edu Website   ∙\bullet   GitHub
Abstract

Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

1 Introduction

Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) learns the state-action value function (Q-function) of a target policy from an offline dataset collected by a different behavior policy, which enables RL to reuse logged experience in real-world domains such as robotics (Levine et al., 2016; Kalashnikov et al., 2018) and industrial control (Zhan et al., 2022). However, off-policy value learning becomes harder as the effective horizon grows (Laidlaw et al., 2023), i.e., the number of transitions across which the critic must carry value information before reaching a state whose value it already knows. Most off-policy actor-critic methods learn the critic with one-step temporal-difference (TD) backups (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025c). A one-step target bootstraps after a single logged transition, which makes it robust to off-policy data but moves value back by only one transition per update. We show that the value error at a state is exactly the sum of the one-step Bellman residuals along the rest of the trajectory, so a critic can reach a small TD loss and still misvalue the start states by an amount that grows with the horizon.

Multi-step returns (Watkins, 1989; Sutton and Barto, 2018) or Q-chunking (Li et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2023) shorten this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps before bootstrapping. Nevertheless, this imposes a trade-off between fast value propagation (longer backups) and low off-policy bias (shorter backups): we show that each spanned suboptimal action adds a systematic bias that grows toward a limit linear in HH. Since offline trajectories could be mixed with suboptimal actions, no fixed backup length is optimal for every TD update. Per-decision off-policy corrections such as Retrace (Precup et al., 2000; Munos et al., 2016) make this choice at every transition with importance ratios. However, these ratios require policy densities, which flow or diffusion-based policies (Park et al., 2025c; Mao et al., 2024a; Li and Levine, 2026; Xu et al., 2026) do not expose.

In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), which shortens the effective horizon of Q-learning without inheriting the bias of suboptimal dataset actions. HQL achieves this by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns at every transition (Figure 1). More specifically, HQL attaches a binary gate to every logged action, i.e., every action stored in the dataset: if the target critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-NN actions sampled from the BC policy, the gate is open and the target continues through it for one more step; otherwise, the target falls back to a one-step bootstrap. Our key observation is that this gate is principled without any density: for the optimal policy π∝μ​exp⁡(τ​Q)\pi\propto\mu\exp(\tau Q) that behavior-regularized RL approximates (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2025b), the behavior density cancels from the importance ratio, and as τ→∞\tau\to\infty the largest gate that preserves QπQ^{\pi} becomes exactly the comparison of critic values. HQL uses an estimated behavior model only to sample action candidates and never evaluates its density. Since the gate depends only on the ordering of critic values, it is also invariant to the reward scale, and the only hyperparameter in HQL is the number of candidates NN.

We evaluate HQL on a combination-lock task, whose true QQ-values are known exactly, and on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks (Park et al., 2025a; Park and Levine, 2026). On the combination lock, HQL keeps the lowest value estimation error across different horizon, whereas one-step TD accumulates error and nn-step TD fails on corrupted dataset. On OGBench and OCBench, at a matched budget of critic targets, HQL outperforms one-step TD, nn-step TD, Q-chunking (Li et al., 2025b), and Long-horizon Q-Learning (Abraham et al., 2026), especially on the most challenging long-horizon tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that most of HQL’s targets are one or few-step targets: HQL wins by choosing which targets to extend, not by extending them far.

2 Related Work

Error propagation in value learning.

Error propagation through bootstrapping has been studied for approximate value and policy iteration (Munos, 2005; Farahmand et al., 2010), TD with function approximation (Tsitsiklis and Roy, 1997), and nn-step and TD(λ\lambda) updates (Kearns and Singh, 2000); its instability with off-policy data is the deadly triad (van Hasselt et al., 2018), and the horizon governs the difficulty of evaluation and learning (Liu et al., 2018; Laidlaw et al., 2023).

Multi-step off-policy correction.

Multi-step returns and eligibility traces shorten the backup chain (Watkins, 1989; Sutton and Barto, 2018; De Asis et al., 2018), and a small fixed nn is standard in deep RL (Hessel et al., 2018; Kapturowski et al., 2019; Hernandez-Garcia and Sutton, 2019). Per-decision importance sampling (Precup et al., 2000) and its clipped variants (Retrace (Munos et al., 2016; Touati et al., 2018), off-policy Q⁡(λ)Q(\lambda) (Harutyunyan et al., 2016), V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018), trajectory-aware traces (Daley et al., 2023)) correct the mismatch step by step, and emphatic TD reweights updates (Sutton et al., 2016). Watkins’s Q⁡(λ)Q(\lambda) cuts traces at non-greedy actions while Peng’s Q⁡(λ)Q(\lambda) keeps them (Peng and Williams, 1996; Kozuno et al., 2021; Kim and hwan Oh, 2026); other work adapts the trace (White and White, 2016; Rowland et al., 2020), avoids ratios via action-dependent bootstrapping (Mahmood et al., 2017), gates traces at non-greedy actions (Daley, 2026), or adds multi-step inequalities (Abraham et al., 2026). However, these corrections need action probabilities or a discrete greedy target policy.

Horizon reduction.

Instead of correcting within a backup, horizon-reduction methods change what a decision is. Hierarchical methods act over options or subgoals (Bacon et al., 2017; Vezhnevets et al., 2017; Nachum et al., 2018; Nachum et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022), and action chunking treats a short action sequence as one decision (Seo and Abbeel, 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2026). However, within each segment they use a fixed, uncorrected backup and inherit the bias; HQL is orthogonal and contains both as ungated special cases. Another line exploits the structure of goal-reaching tasks through quasimetric value functions (Wang et al., 2023a; Zheng et al., 2026), graph search over subgoals (Eysenbach et al., 2019), and goal-conditioned hierarchies (Park et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2025; Zhou and Kao, 2025; Park et al., 2026). These methods rely on a goal-reaching reward and thus apply only to goal-conditioned RL; in contrast, HQL makes no assumption on the reward.

Policy extraction with expressive policies.

Offline RL methods regularize the policy toward the data, either explicitly through divergence penalties (Wu et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) or implicitly through in-sample value learning and weighted behavior cloning (Peng et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025a). Recent work extracts expressive diffusion or flow policies by value-guided training (Wang et al., 2023b; Mao et al., 2024a; Park et al., 2025c), rejection sampling from a behavior model (Chen et al., 2023; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023), adjoint matching (Li and Levine, 2026), or value gradient flow (Xu et al., 2026). These methods keep a one-step critic; HQL only changes the critic’s target and can serve any of them.

3 Preliminaries

We consider the problem presented as a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r,H)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,H), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} are the state and action spaces, P⁡(s′|s,a)P(s^{\prime}|s,a) and r⁡(s,a)r(s,a) denote the transition dynamics and reward function, and HH is the horizon; an episode that reaches its goal early enters a zero-reward absorbing state, so every episode has length HH. For a policy π⁡(a|s)\pi(a|s), the action value is Qπ(s,a)=𝔼π[∑tr(st,at)∣s0=s,a0=a]Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a], with Vπ(s)=𝔼a∼π(⋅|s)[Qπ(s,a)]V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[Q^{\pi}(s,a)] and advantage Aπ​(s,a)=Qπ​(s,a)−Vπ​(s)A^{\pi}(s,a)=Q^{\pi}(s,a)-V^{\pi}(s). We consider the off-policy setting, where one needs to estimate QπQ^{\pi} of a target policy π\pi from a dataset (or replay buffer) 𝒟\mathcal{D} collected by a possibly suboptimal behavior policy μ⁡(a|s)\mu(a|s).

3.1 Error Accumulation in One-Step and nn-Step TD

Error decomposition along a chain.

To understand how critic error scales with the horizon, we derive one error law for one-step and nn-step backups (derivations in Appendices A.1–A.2). Consider the deterministic chain s0→s1→⋯→sHs_{0}\rightarrow s_{1}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow s_{H} induced by a fixed deterministic target policy, with an exactly known terminal value. Write Qt=Q⁡(st,at)Q_{t}=Q(s_{t},a_{t}), let rtr_{t} be the reward on the transition out of sts_{t}, and let Q¯\overline{Q} be the target critic, with V¯π(s)=𝔼a∼π(⋅|s)[Q¯(s,a)]\overline{V}^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[\overline{Q}(s,a)]. The nn-step target is

Yt(n)=∑j=0n−1rt+j+V¯π​(st+n),Y_{t}^{(n)}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r_{t+j}+\overline{V}^{\pi}(s_{t+n}), (1)

where a true terminal state replaces the last term by its known value. The loss at lookahead nn is LTD(n)=𝔼t​[(Qt−sg⁡(Yt(n)))2]L^{(n)}_{\mathrm{TD}}=\mathbb{E}_{t}[(Q_{t}-\operatorname{sg}(Y_{t}^{(n)}))^{2}], where sg\operatorname{sg} stops gradients (Sutton and Barto, 2018); for n=1n=1 we write LTDL_{\mathrm{TD}}. With the one-step Bellman residual et=Qt−rt−Qt+1e_{t}=Q_{t}-r_{t}-Q_{t+1} and the value error ϵt=Qt−Qtπ\epsilon_{t}=Q_{t}-Q_{t}^{\pi}, we have et=ϵt−ϵt+1e_{t}=\epsilon_{t}-\epsilon_{t+1} because Qtπ=rt+Qt+1πQ_{t}^{\pi}=r_{t}+Q_{t+1}^{\pi}, and with an exact terminal value (ϵH=0\epsilon_{H}=0) the recursion telescopes:

ϵt=∑τ=tH−1eτ.\epsilon_{t}=\sum_{\tau=t}^{H-1}e_{\tau}. (2)

In other words, the value error is exactly the sum of the downstream residuals, for any critic at any point in training.

A unified error law.

To see how the residuals add up, we model them as random noise across training runs: each residual has zero mean and variance σ2\sigma^{2}, and residuals at different steps are only weakly correlated (Appendix A.1). Under this model, applying Eq. 2 to nn-step backups, one block of nn steps at a time, gives a single expression for the start-state error (Appendix A.2):

RMSE⁡(ϵ0)2≈Hn​LTD(n)⏟residual accumulation+(1−1n)2​H2​A¯μ2⏟behavior-action bias,\operatorname{RMSE}(\epsilon_{0})^{2}\;\approx\;\underbrace{\frac{H}{n}\,L^{(n)}_{\mathrm{TD}}}_{\text{residual accumulation}}\;+\;\underbrace{\left(1-\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^{\!2}H^{2}\,\bar{A}_{\mu}^{2}}_{\text{behavior-action bias}}, (3)

where A¯μ≤0\bar{A}_{\mu}\leq 0 is the average advantage of the logged actions that the targets span. Intuitively, the first term decreases with nn while the second increases with nn, so a longer backup trades residual accumulation for behavior-action bias.

One-step TD: residuals accumulate as Θ⁡(H)\Theta(\sqrt{H}).

A one-step target spans no logged action, so the bias term vanishes, and summing Eq. 2 under the residual model gives, as H−t→∞H-t\to\infty,

RMSE⁡(ϵt)=𝔼⁡[ϵt2]∼σeff​H−t,\operatorname{RMSE}(\epsilon_{t})=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{t}^{2}]}\sim\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}\sqrt{H-t}, (4)

with σeff2=σ2+2​∑ℓ≥1Cov⁡(et,et+ℓ)\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=\sigma^{2}+2\sum_{\ell\geq 1}\operatorname{Cov}(e_{t},e_{t+\ell}) the long-run variance of the residuals. This result is important as it shows that a small training loss does not certify a small value error: since LTD=𝔼⁡[et2]=σ2L_{\mathrm{TD}}=\mathbb{E}[e_{t}^{2}]=\sigma^{2} measures only the per-step residual, Eq. 3 at n=1n=1 reads

RMSE⁡(ϵ0)=H​LTD\operatorname{RMSE}(\epsilon_{0})=\sqrt{H\,L_{\mathrm{TD}}} (5)

up to the factor σeff/σ\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/\sigma. Appendix A.1 discusses when this rate fails and how a discount γ<1\gamma<1 caps it at a horizon of order 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma).

nn-step TD: bias grows toward H​|A¯μ|H|\bar{A}_{\mu}|.

Bootstrapping nn steps ahead divides the residual term by nn. However, along a logged trajectory Yt(n)Y_{t}^{(n)} now deviates from Qπ​(st,at)Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a_{t}) by ∑j=1n−1Aπ​(st+j,at+j)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A^{\pi}(s_{t+j},a_{t+j}) plus the bootstrap error at the endpoint (Eq. 14). For a near-optimal target policy every spanned advantage is at most zero, so this bias is systematic and does not average out; as nn grows, the square root of the second term of Eq. 3 approaches H​|A¯μ|H|\bar{A}_{\mu}|. This indicates that no fixed nn suits all logged actions: the best lookahead nn changes from step to step, which calls for a per-transition rule to minimize the total error.

4 Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning

In this section, we introduce Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL). We begin with a gated multi-step target and design the gate based on value comparison (Section 4.1). We then show that this gate is a limiting case of per-decision importance sampling yet needs no action density (Section 4.2). Finally, we provide several practical considerations for HQL and discuss its connection to previous work (Section 4.3).

4.1 Gated Multi-Step Targets

Our key idea is to let a backup continue through a logged action only when that action is at least as good as the actions the target policy would take, i.e., its advantage under the target policy is non-negative, which keeps it out of the bias term of Eq. 3 while reducing the horizon of TD learning via multi-step bootstrapping. To do so, we attach a gate ci∈{0,1}c_{i}\in\{0,1\} to every transition and define the HQL target backward along a logged segment,

Ythql=rt+γ​V¯π​(st+1)⏟one-step target+γ​ct+1​(Yt+1hql−Q¯​(st+1,at+1))⏟downstream correction,Y_{t}^{\textsc{hql}}=\underbrace{r_{t}+\gamma\,\overline{V}^{\pi}(s_{t+1})}_{\text{one-step target}}\;+\;\gamma\,c_{t+1}\underbrace{\big(Y_{t+1}^{\textsc{hql}}-\overline{Q}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\big)}_{\text{downstream correction}}, (6)

with the correction set to zero at the end of the segment, and γ\gamma kept for generality. Intuitively, the first term is the usual one-step bootstrap from the target policy, and the second term carries back whatever the logged continuation has learned beyond the critic’s current estimate at (st+1,at+1)(s_{t+1},a_{t+1}). When the gate accepts at+1a_{t+1}, this correction flows back and the target extends one more step; when it rejects at+1a_{t+1}, the target is a plain one-step target, and the states after the cut still start their own targets (as shown in Figure 1, bottom). Unrolling the recursion, a run of accepted actions yields a multi-step target whose length is set by the data rather than fixed in advance. Note that c≡0c\equiv 0 recovers one-step TD and c≡1c\equiv 1 is the uncorrected multi-step return.

It remains to decide when the gate is open, i.e., whether the target policy would keep the logged action. Intuitively, a logged action is safe to follow if it is at least as good as what the policy itself would propose, which the critic can check by comparing the logged action with candidates drawn from the policy’s own sampler:

ci=𝕀[Q¯(si,ai)≥max1≤m≤NQ¯(si,ai(m))],ai(m)∼μ(⋅|si),c_{i}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\overline{Q}(s_{i},a_{i})\;\geq\;\max_{1\leq m\leq N}\overline{Q}\big(s_{i},a_{i}^{(m)}\big)\right],\qquad a_{i}^{(m)}\sim\mu(\cdot|s_{i}), (7)

where μ\mu is the behavior policy that can be estimated using any advanced generative models from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. In other words, the logged action is kept if it is at least as good as the best of NN policy proposals. Note that the gate depends only on an ordering of critic values, so it is invariant to the scale of QQ, needs no behavior density, and has NN as its only hyperparameter; it costs NN behavior samples and critic evaluations per transition, the same as the best-of-NN bootstrap already requires.

4.2 A Density-Free Gate via Per-Decision Importance Sampling

A remaining question is whether cutting multi-step backups with this gate is principled, since cutting changes what a multi-step backup converges to. Per-decision importance sampling answers this (Precup et al., 2000; Munos et al., 2016): in the tabular setting, any gate ci∈[0,1]c_{i}\in[0,1] with ci≤π⁡(ai|si)/μ⁡(ai|si)c_{i}\leq\pi(a_{i}|s_{i})/\mu(a_{i}|s_{i}) preserves QπQ^{\pi} as the fixed point of Eq. 6, and we call such a gate valid. However, evaluating this bound requires the density ratio π/μ\pi/\mu, which is unavailable and hard to estimate (Mao et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2025a) when using generative policies, or when policies are implicit, e.g., μ\mu is a flow sampler and π\pi selects among its samples. Fortunately, the ratio has a closed form for the policy that behavior-regularized RL methods approximate, i.e., the exponential tilt of the behavior policy (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023; Li and Levine, 2026),

πθ(a|s)=μ⁡(a|s)​exp⁡(τ​Q​(s,a))Z⁡(s),Z(s)=𝔼a∼μ(⋅|s)[exp(τQ(s,a))],\pi_{\theta}(a|s)=\frac{\mu(a|s)\exp(\tau Q(s,a))}{Z(s)},\qquad Z(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\mu(\cdot|s)}\left[\exp(\tau Q(s,a))\right], (8)

so the behavior density cancels and log⁡(π/μ)​(ai|si)=τ​Q​(si,ai)−log⁡Z⁡(si)\log(\pi/\mu)(a_{i}|s_{i})=\tau Q(s_{i},a_{i})-\log Z(s_{i}). We estimate the normalizer from NN behavior samples as log⁡Z^​(si)=LSEm⁡(τ​Q¯​(si,ai(m)))−log⁡N\widehat{\log Z}(s_{i})=\operatorname{LSE}_{m}(\tau\overline{Q}(s_{i},a_{i}^{(m)}))-\log N, where LSEm(xm)=log∑m=1Nexp(xm)\operatorname{LSE}_{m}(x_{m})=\log\sum_{m=1}^{N}\exp(x_{m}) is the log-sum-exp, and clipping the ratio at one gives the largest valid gate

ci=exp⁡(min⁡{0,τ​Q¯​(si,ai)−log⁡Z^​(si)}).c_{i}=\exp\left(\min\left\{0,\,\tau\overline{Q}(s_{i},a_{i})-\widehat{\log Z}(s_{i})\right\}\right). (9)

This soft gate interpolates between two extremes. As τ→0\tau\to 0, every gate equals one and the target is an uncorrected multi-step return. As τ→∞\tau\to\infty, the tilt concentrates on the best behavior-supported action, and because LSEm⁡(xm)≤maxm⁡xm+log⁡N\operatorname{LSE}_{m}(x_{m})\leq\max_{m}x_{m}+\log N, the exponent is nonnegative at any τ\tau when no candidate beats the logged action and tends to −∞-\infty otherwise, so the soft gate becomes exactly the value comparison of Eq. 7. Therefore, HQL’s gate is the τ→∞\tau\to\infty limit of a valid gate, which is more scalable and robust since it avoids a temperature and can be computed without density. It also outperforms the soft gate at every τ\tau we tried (Appendix A.7).

4.3 Practical Considerations

Dense targets over a trajectory window.

Since HQL is not restricted to a fixed nn-step backup, it does not need to compute a target only at the first state of a sampled segment. Instead, HQL samples a trajectory window (st,at,rt,…,st+H)(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t},\dots,s_{t+H}) of HH consecutive transitions and computes the gated multi-step target for every state–action pair in the window. More specifically, it computes the gates cic_{i} once at every position, evaluates Eq. 6 backward from the window end, and regresses each (st+j,at+j)(s_{t+j},a_{t+j}) onto its own target Yt+jhqlY_{t+j}^{\textsc{hql}}, j=0,…,H−1j=0,\dots,H-1, masking positions beyond an episode boundary (Algorithm 1). By doing so, a window yields HH targets whose maximal reach decreases from HH to 11, and the gate can shorten each of them further. To enable a fair comparison, we hold the number of critic targets per update fixed: with a budget of BB, one-step TD samples BB transitions and HQL samples B/HB/H windows.

Multi-step decisions via Chunked-HQL.

So far the decision stride is fixed to 1, meaning each decision corresponds to a single environment step. To allow for more flexible decision-making, we let one decision span several environment steps. More specifically, with stride LL, a decision is a chunk of LL primitive actions that the critic scores as a unit, Q(st,at:t+L)Q(s_{t},a_{t:t+L}), and a window of HH chunks reaches L⋅HL\!\cdot\!H environment steps while still producing HH targets. Note that the gate is unchanged, now comparing the logged chunk with the best-of-NN chunks drawn from the policy, and the backup of Eq. 6 holds with γL\gamma^{L} in place of γ\gamma and per-chunk reward sums.

Connections to existing methods.

To summarize, in HQL or Chunked-HQL, LL sets how many environment steps one decision covers, and HH sets how many decisions one target may chain (Figure 2). With L=1L{=}1, H=1H{=}1 gives one-step TD, an ungated window of size HH gives uncorrected HH-step TD, and a gated window gives HQL. With L=kL{=}k, H=1H{=}1 is Q-chunking with chunks of kk actions (Li et al., 2025b), since a single chunk leaves nothing to gate, and H>1H{>}1 gives Chunked-HQL at stride kk. Note that the two variables extend the maximal reach of a target, L⋅HL\cdot H environment steps, in different ways. Increasing HH lets one target makes more decisions while the policy outputs less actions per step, and the gate decides for each target how many of these decisions it actually uses. In contrast, increasing LL makes each decision cover more environment steps, but each chunk then runs open loop and the policy must search a larger, L⋅dim(𝒜)L\cdot\dim(\mathcal{A})-dimensional action space.

5 Experiments

The goal of our experiments is to answer four questions. (Q1) Does HQL enable better value learning under different horizon lengths and dataset suboptimality? (Q2) How does HQL compare with TD and other baselines on OGBench and OCBench? (Q3) Does HQL work with different policy-extraction methods? (Q4) How do the different components of HQL affect its performance?

5.1 Experimental Setup

Combination lock.

For Q1, we use a modified combination-lock chain (Park et al., 2025b) with H linearly ordered states and two actions: the “correct” one advances to the next state and the other returns to the first state, with reward -1 per step and 0 at the terminal state. The offline dataset consists of length-n=64 windows (64 transitions each): for every state–action pair we roll out M=100 windows that start with that pair and then follow the correct action, truncating a window early if it reaches the terminal state. Following Park et al. (2025b), we construct datasets of nn-step trajectory windows with uniform coverage of starting state-action pairs. To study the effect of increasing action corruption, we independently replace each of the n−1=63n-1=63 subsequent actions with the non-optimal action with probability p∈{0,0.002,0.005,0.011,0.022}p\in\{0,0.002,0.005,0.011,0.022\}, chosen so that in expectation (1−p)63∈{100,88,73,50,25}%(1-p)^{63}\in\{100,88,73,50,25\}\% of windows are clean, i.e. contain no corrupted action. We use H∈{512,1024,2048,4096}H\in\{512,1024,2048,4096\}, giving 2HM windows per dataset. Because the dynamics are deterministic, the ground-truth Q is available in closed form (A.3).

OGBench.

Q2–Q4 use six state-based OGBench configurations (Park et al., 2025a): cube-double, cube-triple, scene (sparse reward), humanoidmaze-medium, antmaze-giant and humanoidmaze-giant, whose task horizons last 500500 to 40004000 steps (Table 5); we report the mean score over each configuration’s five tasks. Runs train for 1M offline and then 1M online steps, with 5050 evaluation episodes every 10510^{5} steps; a run’s score is the mean of its last three evaluations.

OCBench.

To test HQL on even longer horizons, we also use OCBench (Park and Levine, 2026), a robotic manipulation benchmark whose datasets come from scripted policies with properties similar to human demonstrations. We take eight full-frequency (5050 Hz) tasks from four domains (block, chamber, switch, hanoi), whose episodes last 10001000 to 50005000 steps. Following the RL baselines of OCBench, all methods use 2525-step action chunks, 8×20488\times 2048 residual MLPs, an HL-Gauss critic and γ=0.9999\gamma{=}0.9999, with 10241024 critic targets per update. Runs train for 1M offline and 1.5M online steps with 500500 evaluation episodes every 5×1045\times 10^{4} steps (Appendix A.6).

Baselines.

We compare HQL (H=16H=16) with existing baselines under a matched compute budget: every method receives 512512 critic targets per gradient step. We consider three TD baselines. 16-window TD uses the same windows and batch as HQL but removes the gate, so comparing the two isolates the gate’s effect. 8-step TD (n=8n{=}8 matches the average reach of a 1616-step window) and 1-step TD each regress a single target per sequence with a batch of 512512. We also compare with Q-chunking (QC) (Li et al., 2025b), which treats a chunk of 88 actions as a single decision and bears no off-policy bias, and Long-horizon Q-Learning (LQL) (Abraham et al., 2026), which adds hinge penalties to one-step TD that enforce multi-step inequalities along the logged trajectory. All methods share the same critic architecture and use the same behavior flow policy with best-of-N sampling.

5.2 Q1: A Toy Example with Corrupted Windows

Figure 3 supports both halves of the analysis. On clean data, the error of 1-step TD grows by three orders of magnitude from H=512H{=}512 to 40964096, while 64-step TD and HQL avoid this accumulation. As the corruption rate increases, 64-step TD degrades sharply, because each target sums the negative advantages of the actions it spans. HQL cuts the trace at those actions: its error stays below both 1-step TD and 64-step TD at every horizon.

5.3 Q2: Results on OGBench and OCBench

HQL is the strongest method across all six domains.

HQL reaches a mean success rate of 0.74 against 0.49 for the best TD baseline, 8-step TD (Figure 5). Consistent with our analysis in Section 3.1, the gap is largest on the four configurations with the largest horizons of 1000 steps or more (Table 5); on cube-triple, HQL reaches 0.54 while both multi-step baselines score 0. 16-window TD matches HQL in everything except the gate, yet it is the weakest method on average, this demonstrates the effectiveness of gating in HQL.

Comparison with other baselines.

At the same budget and sampling width (Table 1), HQL improves the mean success rate by 12%12\% over LQL and by 29%29\% over QC. QC is best on cube-double and scene but scores 0%0\% on both humanoid mazes.

Although Q-chunking avoids the off-policy bias by having the critic to score the whole L-sized action chunk Q(st,at:t+L)Q(s_{t},a_{t:t+L}), it falls short because the critic must choose among L⋅dim⁡(𝒜)L\cdot\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A})-dimensional chunks, and a fixed best-of-NN search covers that space increasingly sparsely as the chunk size LL grows. Second, each chunk runs open loop for LL-steps (we choose L=8L=8 while running QC), so the agent cannot correct its action within a chunk. This also explains why QC performs well on cube-double and scene, whose chunks are low-dimensional (please refer to table 5 for action dimensions of the different OGBench tasks), but trails on antmaze-giant and fails on both humanoid mazes. We expect a wider best-of-NN search to help QC, since it covers the chunk space more densely, though at a cost in samples and critic evaluations that grows with NN. The gate is also complementary to chunking: adding it on top of chunked actions (Chunked-HQL) raises QC’s success rate from 45%45\% to 81%81\% (Table 1).

Why does HQL help?

One might expect a multi-step method to win by sending reward information far back along the trajectory. To understand why HQL works better than the TD baselines, we log how many steps each target’s trace survives (Figure 7). Perhaps surprisingly, the actual traces are short: 77%77\% of targets are exactly one-step targets while 17%17\% extend to two steps and 6%6\% to three or more steps, and none exceeds six of the sixteen available steps. This indicates that HQL helps not by making targets longer but by choosing which ones to extend: nn-step TD extends all of them and inherits the bias of every action spanned, 1-step TD extends none, and HQL extends a target only when its logged action passes the gate.

Chunked-HQL scales to the longer horizons of OCBench.

On OCBench, we compare Chunked-HQL (L=25L{=}25, H=8H{=}8, i.e., a 200200-step window) with nn-step TD at n∈{100,200}n\in\{100,200\}, which regresses the chunk critic onto an uncorrected nn-step return and is the backup used by OCBench’s own RL baselines (n=200n{=}200). Motivated by Section 5.5, we decouple the two widths of HQL: the gate uses N=2N{=}2, while the bootstrap and acting use best-of-1616 as in the baselines. Chunked-HQL reaches a mean success rate of 0.820.82 at 2.52.5M steps against 0.530.53 for 100-step TD and 0.460.46 for 200-step TD (Figure 5). The gap is largest on switch-3x3 (0.910.91 vs. 0.150.15), switch-4x4 (0.760.76 vs. 0.170.17) and chamber-medium (0.530.53 vs. 0.120.12), where the nn-step baselines barely improve or even degrade during online training. Note that 200-step TD is worse than 100-step TD on seven of the eight tasks, which agrees with Eq. 3: a longer uncorrected return sums the negative advantages of more logged actions, while the gate lets HQL extend a target only through chunks that pass the value comparison.

5.4 Q3: Combining HQL with Other Policy Extraction Methods

HQL with QAM.

Q-learning with adjoint matching (QAM) (Li and Levine, 2026) trains a flow policy to sample from the tilted distribution π∝μ​exp⁡(τ​Q)\pi\propto\mu\exp(\tau Q). To combine it with HQL, we keep the hard gate unchanged and only replace the best-of-NN policy with the QAM policy. With HQL as its critic, QAM improves on all four tasks at the end of online training, especially on cube-triple (1%→80%1\%\to 80\%) and humanoidmaze-giant (0%→63%0\%\to 63\%).

HQL with value gradient flow (VGF).

VGF (Xu et al., 2026) can be thought of an implicit policy that transports from behavior samples toward high-value actions with a few steps of QQ-gradient ascent. With HQL as its critic, VGF again improves on all four tasks, most on antmaze-giant (28%→90%28\%\to 90\%).

5.5 Q4: Ablations of HQL

Does the window length HH matter?

We find the effect is small. At a fixed budget of 512512 targets per update, H∈{8,16,32}H\in\{8,16,32\} (batch 64/32/1664/32/16) gives similar performance: 0.6070.607, 0.6460.646, and 0.6210.621 (Figure 7, left). This agrees with the trace length analysis in Section 5.3: since empirically no target used more than six steps, a window of 1616 already exceeds what the gate uses. HQL is therefore not sensitive to HH unless it is too small.

Does the best-of-NN width matter for HQL?

We try best-of-NN width from {4,8,16}\{4,8,16\}. On OGBench datasets we find that a smaller NN is better: N∈{4,8,16}N\in\{4,8,16\} gives the mean value of 0.5960.596, 0.5210.521, and 0.4610.461, three times the spread of HH (Figure 7, right). Intuitively, a logged action exchangeable with the NN proposals beats all of them with probability 1/(N+1)1/(N{+}1), so a larger NN accepts fewer logged actions and HQL approaches 1-step TD when NN is large. We provide more details on the ablation setup in Appendix A.8.

6 Conclusion and Limitations

In this paper, we propose HQL, which shortens the effective horizon of Q-learning without inheriting the bias of suboptimal logged actions. HQL gates each logged action with a density-free value comparison and achieves strong results on long-horizon OGBench tasks, both alone and as a drop-in critic for QAM and VGF. We believe that HQL represents a concrete step toward horizon-scalable off-policy RL. One limitation is that the gate relies on the critic’s own ranking. One future work is to apply HQL over subgoals in a hierarchical manner.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Derivation of the One-Step Error Accumulation

This appendix states the residual model behind Eq. 4 and derives the rate. For a family of chains with growing horizon, assume the one-step residuals et=Qt−rt−Qt+1e_{t}=Q_{t}-r_{t}-Q_{t+1} form a second-order stationary process whose statistics do not depend on HH:

𝔼⁡[et]=0,Var⁡(et)=σ2,C⁡(ℓ)=Cov⁡(et,et+ℓ),\mathbb{E}[e_{t}]=0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(e_{t})=\sigma^{2},\qquad C(\ell)=\operatorname{Cov}(e_{t},e_{t+\ell}), (10)

with weak correlation in the form ∑ℓ=1∞|C⁡(ℓ)|<∞\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}|C(\ell)|<\infty. Taking the mean and variance of the sum in Eq. 2 with n=H−tn=H-t terms gives

𝔼⁡[ϵt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{t}] =0,\displaystyle=0, (11)
Var⁡(ϵt)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{t}) =n​σ2+2​∑ℓ=1n−1(n−ℓ)​C​(ℓ).\displaystyle=n\sigma^{2}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-1}(n-\ell)C(\ell). (12)

By summability of |C⁡(ℓ)||C(\ell)|, as n→∞n\to\infty,

Var⁡(ϵt)n⟶σeff2:=σ2+2​∑ℓ=1∞C⁡(ℓ),\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{t})}{n}\longrightarrow\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}:=\sigma^{2}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}C(\ell), (13)

the long-run variance, which is necessarily nonnegative. If σeff2>0\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}>0, then RMSE⁡(ϵt)∼σeff​H−t\operatorname{RMSE}(\epsilon_{t})\sim\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}\sqrt{H-t}, which is Eq. 4; this is the nondegenerate random-walk regime.

When the rate does not apply.

The random-walk rate is conditional on the residual model and is not a worst case. Negative correlation can give σeff2=0\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=0 and o⁡(H−t)o(\sqrt{H-t}) error, while a systematic same-sign residual of horizon-independent size gives Θ⁡(H)\Theta(H). Such a residual arises, for example, when the critic’s values are shrunk toward zero under all-negative rewards: the semi-gradient fixed point with shrinkage κ\kappa satisfies et=−κ​Qt>0e_{t}=-\kappa Q_{t}>0 at every step. Accumulation also requires persistent residuals: in a fully expressive tabular chain, exact convergence gives Q=QπQ=Q^{\pi}, et=0e_{t}=0, and no accumulation, whereas function approximation, finite optimization, and target-network lag all leave residuals.

Discounting.

With γ<1\gamma<1 the telescoped sum is geometrically weighted, ϵt=∑k=0H−t−1γk​et+k\epsilon_{t}=\sum_{k=0}^{H-t-1}\gamma^{k}e_{t+k}, and for uncorrelated residuals Var⁡(ϵt)=σ2​(1−γ2​(H−t))/(1−γ2)\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{t})=\sigma^{2}(1-\gamma^{2(H-t)})/(1-\gamma^{2}). The factor grows linearly in H−tH-t until H−tH-t is of order 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma) and saturates at 1/(1−γ2)1/(1-\gamma^{2}) afterwards, so the discount caps the accumulation at its own effective horizon (≈100\approx 100 steps at γ=0.995\gamma=0.995) rather than removing it; the analysis applies with HH replaced by min⁡{H,1/(1−γ)}\min\{H,1/(1-\gamma)\} up to constants.

A.2 Derivation of the nn-Step Error Accumulation

Single-target decomposition.

With Aπ​(s,a)=Qπ​(s,a)−Vπ​(s)A^{\pi}(s,a)=Q^{\pi}(s,a)-V^{\pi}(s) and endpoint error ϵV​(s)=V¯π​(s)−Vπ​(s)\epsilon_{V}(s)=\overline{V}^{\pi}(s)-V^{\pi}(s), expanding the target of Eq. 1 over the behavior continuation gives

𝔼μ[Yt(n)−Qπ(st,at)|st,at]=∑j=1n−1𝔼μ[Aπ(st+j,at+j)|st,at]+𝔼μ[ϵV(st+n)|st,at].\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[Y_{t}^{(n)}-Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{t},a_{t}\right]=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[A^{\pi}(s_{t+j},a_{t+j})\,\middle|\,s_{t},a_{t}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\epsilon_{V}(s_{t+n})\,\middle|\,s_{t},a_{t}\right]. (14)

The derivation uses only rt+j+Vπ​(st+j+1)=Qπ​(st+j,at+j)=Vπ​(st+j)+Aπ​(st+j,at+j)r_{t+j}+V^{\pi}(s_{t+j+1})=Q^{\pi}(s_{t+j},a_{t+j})=V^{\pi}(s_{t+j})+A^{\pi}(s_{t+j},a_{t+j}) at each spanned transition (deterministic transitions given the action; the j=0j=0 term contributes no advantage because the target evaluates Qπ​(st,at)Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a_{t}) at the logged action itself). The first term is the behavior-action bias inside the segment, the second the endpoint bootstrap error.

Chaining blocks along the horizon.

To turn the per-target decomposition into a start-state statement, partition the chain into H/nH/n blocks of length nn (assume n|Hn\mid H for clarity) and define the nn-step training residual e~t=Qt−Yt(n)\tilde{e}_{t}=Q_{t}-Y_{t}^{(n)} at each block start. Adding and subtracting QπQ^{\pi} and applying Eq. 14,

ϵt=e~t+bt​(n)+ϵt+n,bt​(n)=∑j=1n−1Aπ​(st+j,at+j),\epsilon_{t}=\tilde{e}_{t}+b_{t}(n)+\epsilon_{t+n},\qquad b_{t}(n)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A^{\pi}(s_{t+j},a_{t+j}), (15)

where we identify the endpoint state-value error with the action-value error at the next block start (exact on the deterministic evaluation chain). Iterating over blocks with ϵH=0\epsilon_{H}=0,

ϵ0=∑j=0H/n−1[e~j​n+bj​n​(n)].\epsilon_{0}=\sum_{j=0}^{H/n-1}\left[\tilde{e}_{jn}+b_{jn}(n)\right]. (16)

Model the training residuals e~j​n\tilde{e}_{jn} as zero-mean, weakly correlated across blocks with per-block variance σn2=LTD(n)\sigma_{n}^{2}=L^{(n)}_{\mathrm{TD}} (the analogue of the model in Appendix A.1); the bias terms bj​n​(n)b_{jn}(n), by contrast, share a sign for a near-optimal target policy and add coherently. Then

RMSE⁡(ϵ0)2≈Hn​σn2+(∑j=0H/n−1bj​n​(n))2,\operatorname{RMSE}(\epsilon_{0})^{2}\approx\frac{H}{n}\,\sigma_{n}^{2}+\Bigg(\sum_{j=0}^{H/n-1}b_{jn}(n)\Bigg)^{\!2}, (17)

and since the bias sum covers all logged actions except the H/nH/n block starts, ∑jbj​n​(n)=(1−1n)​H​A¯μ\sum_{j}b_{jn}(n)=(1-\tfrac{1}{n})H\bar{A}_{\mu} with A¯μ\bar{A}_{\mu} the average spanned advantage, which is Eq. 3. The result is schematic in the same sense as Appendix A.1: it conditions on the residual model, ignores cross terms between residuals and biases, and uses block-aligned targets, but none of these affect the two scalings it exhibits—a H/n\sqrt{H/n} random-walk term and a bias term that grows with nn toward the horizon-linear ceiling H​|A¯μ|H|\bar{A}_{\mu}|.

A.3 Combination-Lock Dataset

In this didactic setup (Figure 8), the policy π\pi is the deterministic answer policy, and the dynamics are deterministic and acyclic under π\pi, so the action-value function QπQ^{\pi} has a closed form. We anchor at the terminal state, Vπ​(sH)=0V^{\pi}(s_{H})=0. The Bellman equation then reduces to the recursion Vπ​(si)=−1+Vπ​(si+1)V^{\pi}(s_{i})=-1+V^{\pi}(s_{i+1}), which unrolls to

Vπ(si)=−(H−i),i=0,…,H−1.V^{\pi}(s_{i})=-(H-i),\qquad i=0,\dots,H-1. (18)

Taking the answer action costs one step and advances the chain. Any other action costs one step and resets to the start. Hence

Qπ​(si,ai⋆)\displaystyle Q^{\pi}(s_{i},a^{\star}_{i}) =−1+Vπ​(si+1)=−(H−i),\displaystyle=-1+V^{\pi}(s_{i+1})=-(H-i), (19)
Qπ​(si,a¯i)\displaystyle Q^{\pi}(s_{i},\bar{a}_{i}) =−1+Vπ​(s0)=−(H+1).\displaystyle=-1+V^{\pi}(s_{0})=-(H+1). (20)

A.4 OGBench Benchmark: Experiment Details and Per-Task Results

This appendix documents the configuration behind the OGBench benchmark figure of Section 5.3 (Figure 5) and reports the per-task curves that its task means aggregate over (Figure 9).

Tasks and datasets.

We use six environment–discount configurations: cube-double, cube-triple, scene, and humanoidmaze-medium at γ=0.99\gamma=0.99, and antmaze-giant and humanoidmaze-giant at γ=0.995\gamma=0.995; Table 5 lists dataset sizes, episode lengths, and dimensionalities. Every group provides five single-task variants that share one dataset and differ only in the reward relabelling, and we run all five, so each panel of Figure 5 aggregates five tasks. scene uses the sparse reward relabelling.

Training runs.

Each run trains for 10610^{6} offline gradient steps followed by 10610^{6} online steps, evaluating every 10510^{5} steps with 50 episodes; the reported score is the mean success rate over the last three evaluations. Each method is run across the five different tasks corresponding to each of the six OGBench environments for five seeds. Curves show the mean over seeds of the task-averaged score, with bands of ±1\pm 1 standard deviation across seeds; we average over tasks before computing seed statistics because per-task success is bimodal, so the across-task spread would swamp seed variance. Figure 9 gives the per-task breakdown.

HQL configuration.

HQL uses a window of H=16H=16 with 32 windows per batch, i.e., 32×16=51232\times 16=512 critic targets per update under the accounting of Section 4.3. The gate is the best-of-NN indicator of Eq. 7 with N=4N=4, computed from the target critic. The policy is a behavior-cloned flow sampler with best-of-NN action selection (N=4N=4) used both for acting and for the bootstrap V¯π\overline{V}^{\pi}, so the gate, the bootstrap, and the actor all refer to the same target policy. Table 4 lists the full configuration.

Baseline configurations.

The three TD baselines share all networks and optimization settings with HQL (Table 4) and differ only in how their 512512 critic targets per update are formed (Table 3).

A.5 Shared Implementation Settings

Unless a later subsection states otherwise, every experiment uses the networks, optimizer and behavior flow sampler of Table 4. All agents are implemented in one JAX codebase with shared replay, evaluation and logging, so two compared methods differ only in the settings named for that comparison.

Matched budget.

All comparisons in Section 5.3 and the window-length ablation of Section 5.5 fix the number of critic targets per update at 512512, following the accounting of Park et al. (2025b): a batch of BB windows of length HH yields B⋅HB\cdot H targets for methods that regress every position, and BB targets for methods that regress only the first state. The number of transitions read per update therefore differs across methods; for example, 8-step TD reads 40964096 transitions to form its 512512 targets.

Compute.

Runs of 2×1062\times 10^{6} steps were executed on 8-GPU A100 and H100 nodes, eight runs per node, at about 150150 iterations/s per run (≈\approx4–6 h per run).

A.6 OCBench Benchmark: Experiment Details

This appendix documents the configuration behind the OCBench results of Section 5.3 (Figure 5). Unlike the OGBench experiments, we follow the RL baselines of OCBench (Park and Levine, 2026) for every setting other than the critic target, so all three methods share the same networks, critic loss, action space and action chunks (Table 6).

Tasks and datasets.

We use eight full-frequency (5050 Hz) tasks, block-single, block-double, chamber-easy, chamber-medium, switch-3x3, switch-4x4, hanoi-single and hanoi-double (all task1), whose episode limits range from 10001000 to 50005000 steps. We train on all episodes of each dataset without filtering for successful ones. Actions are normalized as in OCBench, i.e., the 11st and 9999th percentiles of each action dimension are mapped to ±1\pm 1 and the result is clipped at ±5\pm 5.

Method configurations.

Chunked-HQL uses chunks of L=25L=25 actions and windows of H=8H=8 chunks (200200 environment steps) with 128128 windows per batch, i.e., 128×8=1024128\times 8=1024 critic targets per update. Its gate compares the logged chunk with the best of N=2N=2 policy chunks, while the bootstrap and acting take the best of 1616 chunks, the same width as the baselines. The nn-step TD baselines (n∈{100,200}n\in\{100,200\}) regress a single target per sequence with a batch of 10241024. Each run is evaluated with 500500 episodes every 5×1045\times 10^{4} steps, and the reported score is the mean success rate over the last three evaluations.

A.7 Soft Gate versus Hard Gate

Section 4.2 shows that the hard gate of Eq. 7 is the τ→∞\tau\to\infty limit of the soft gate of Eq. 9. A natural question is whether a finite τ\tau works better, since the soft gate keeps partial credit for logged actions that are close to the best candidate. To answer this, we compare the soft gate at τ∈{0,0.5,1,3,30}\tau\in\{0,0.5,1,3,30\} with HQL’s hard gate on six OGBench configurations with five tasks each. Note that τ=0\tau{=}0 sets every gate to one and recovers uncorrected 88-step TD. All runs use H=8H{=}8, a batch of 128128 windows (10241024 critic targets per update), 11M offline and 11M online steps, and one seed; the soft gate estimates log⁡Z^\log\hat{Z} and acts with 1616 behavior samples, and the hard gate uses N=4N{=}4 for both.

Figure 10 and Table 7 show that the hard gate achieves the best mean success rate (61%61\%), and that the soft gate improves steadily as τ\tau increases (36%→57%36\%\to 57\%), i.e., as it approaches the hard gate. The gap is largest on the long-horizon mazes: on humanoidmaze-medium the hard gate reaches 91%91\% against 77%77\% for the best soft gate, and on antmaze-giant 65%65\% against 58%58\%. The soft gate is only better on cube-double at τ=1\tau{=}1, while scene and puzzle-3x3 end at the same value for every gate. This indicates that the hard gate is not only the limit that removes τ\tau as a hyperparameter, but also the strongest member of the family: a finite τ\tau keeps partial credit for suboptimal logged actions, so the multi-step target inherits part of their bias, which is exactly the failure mode of uncorrected nn-step TD.

A.8 Ablation Details

Both panels of Figure 7 use HQL with the shared settings of Appendix A.5. Each panel averages only over the environment–task cells that were run for every value of the ablated setting, so that only that setting varies within a panel.

Window length HH.

We fix the budget at 512512 critic targets per update, so the number of windows per batch decreases as HH increases (6464, 3232 and 1616 for H=8H{=}8, 1616 and 3232 respectively). The panel covers six environment–discount configurations with five tasks each, i.e., 3030 cells.

Gate width NN.

We run this panel at H=8H{=}8 with 128128 windows per batch, i.e., 10241024 critic targets per update, with two seeds per setting (we use 512512 critic targets everywhere else in the paper). Here NN sets both the number of candidates in the gate and the number of best-of-NN samples used for acting, so the panel varies the two together.
